---
title: "Convert gene symbols between species"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(biobouncer)
```

biobouncer does not convert an identifier from one species to another. It
guards a conversion: it cleans the symbols that go in and checks the ids that
come out. The lookup in between is done here by the
[bioclients](https://www.samuelbharti.com/bioclients/) package, which asks
IMPC for the mouse ortholog of a human gene.

This article converts a column of human gene symbols to mouse genes in three
steps:

1. Clean the human symbols.
2. Look up the mouse ortholog of each symbol.
3. Check the mouse ids, and the species of any id a lookup returns.

## Clean the human symbols

A lookup service can only match the symbol it is given, and a retired or
misspelled symbol may match nothing. Check the column first. `cache` mode
checks each symbol against the HGNC snapshot that ships with the package, and
it needs no network.

```{r}
symbols <- c("TP53", "tp53", "MLL", "BRCA1", "NF1", "OCT4", "NOTAGENE")
res <- check_id(symbols, source_db = "hgnc", how = "cache")
res[c("input", "valid", "suggestion", "version")]
```

`tp53` has the wrong case and `MLL` is a previous symbol of `KMT2A`. Both
suggestions are right. `NOTAGENE` has none. The `version` column is the date
of the HGNC snapshot that gave the answer.

Read the suggestions before you apply them. A suggestion is the successor of
a previous symbol or, when there is none, the approved symbol with the nearest
spelling. The check does not know aliases. `OCT4` is an alias of `POU5F1`, and
its suggestion here is `CCT4`, a different gene.

Reject the suggestions that are wrong, then apply the others. One pass over
the result gives the repaired column and the rows to set aside.

```{r}
reject <- "OCT4"

fixable <- res$valid %in% FALSE &
  !is.na(res$suggestion) &
  !res$input %in% reject
clean <- ifelse(fixable, res$suggestion, res$input)
keep <- res$valid %in% TRUE | fixable

human <- unique(clean[keep])
human

clean[!keep]
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
# The lookup output below was pasted from a run on exactly these symbols. A
# new HGNC snapshot that changes them must fail the build here, so the page
# cannot contradict itself.
stopifnot(identical(human, c("TP53", "KMT2A", "BRCA1", "NF1")))
```

## Look up the mouse orthologs

`impc_mouse_ortholog()` from bioclients takes one human symbol. It returns the
MGI id and the mouse symbol that IMPC holds for that gene. The call needs a
network, so the code is shown with the output of a run on 2026-11-15.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(bioclients)

lookup <- function(symbol) {
  res <- impc_mouse_ortholog(symbol)
  if (!res$ok && res$status != "no_data") {
    stop("IMPC lookup failed for ", symbol, ": ", res$status)
  }
  hit <- res$data
  if (is.null(hit)) {
    hit <- data.frame(mgi = NA_character_, marker_symbol = NA_character_)
  }
  cbind(human = symbol, hit)
}

orthologs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(human, lookup))
orthologs
#>   human        mgi marker_symbol
#> 1  TP53  MGI:98834         Trp53
#> 2 KMT2A  MGI:96995         Kmt2a
#> 3 BRCA1 MGI:104537         Brca1
#> 4   NF1  MGI:97306           Nf1
```

When IMPC has no mouse ortholog for a gene, the status is `no_data` and the
helper writes a row of `NA`, so the table keeps one row per human symbol. Any
other failure stops the run. A timeout cannot pass for a missing ortholog.

## Check MGI ids

`impc_mouse_ortholog()` returns only ids that have the MGI shape, so a check
on its output always passes. The `mgi` source does its work on MGI ids that
arrive from a file or a hand-edited table, where a bare number or a lowercase
prefix is common.

```{r}
mgi_ids <- c("MGI:98834", "98834", "mgi:96995")
res <- check_id(mgi_ids, source_db = "mgi")
res[c("input", "valid", "suggestion")]
```

`mgi` has `pattern` mode only. A pass confirms the shape of the id. It does
not confirm that MGI holds a record for it.

## Keep mouse symbols out of the HGNC check

The `hgnc` source holds human symbols only, and biobouncer has no source for
mouse symbols. In `cache` mode, a mouse symbol that is spelled differently
from the human one is not valid, and its suggestion is the human gene.

```{r}
res <- check_id(c("Trp53", "Kmt2a", "Nf1"), source_db = "hgnc", how = "cache")
res[c("input", "valid", "suggestion")]
```

`repair_id()` on this column would turn these mouse symbols into human ones.
A mouse symbol with the same spelling as a human symbol, such as `C3`, passes.
In both cases the result says nothing about the mouse gene. Check a mouse gene
by its MGI id.

## Catch an answer from the wrong species

A lookup can answer for a species you did not ask for. `mygene_genes()` from
bioclients searches human genes unless `species` says otherwise. Given two
mouse symbols and no `species`, it returns the human genes.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
hits <- biohttp::body_or_null(mygene_genes(c("Trp53", "Kmt2a")))
hits[c("symbol", "ensembl_gene")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   symbol ensembl_gene
#>   <chr>  <chr>
#> 1 TP53   ENSG00000141510
#> 2 KMT2A  ENSG00000118058
```

An Ensembl gene id carries its species in the letters after `ENS`, so
biobouncer can test the species offline. Both ids above are well-formed
Ensembl ids, and both fail a check for mouse.

```{r}
is_valid_id(
  c("ENSG00000141510", "ENSG00000118058"),
  source_db = "ensembl",
  species = "mus_musculus"
)
```

The mouse gene id for Trp53 passes the same check.

```{r}
is_valid_id("ENSMUSG00000059552", source_db = "ensembl", species = "mus_musculus")
```

Write the species as a name in this form, or as an NCBI taxon id such as
`10090`. The Ensembl source checks eight species: `homo_sapiens`,
`mus_musculus`, `rattus_norvegicus`, `danio_rerio`, `gallus_gallus`,
`bos_taurus`, `sus_scrofa`, and `canis_lupus_familiaris`. A species outside
that list is not checked, so a name such as `"mouse"` passes every well-formed
id.

## Genome assemblies

A gene symbol and an MGI id name a gene, and neither changes with the genome
assembly. Coordinates do. To test a coordinate against a build, see
[Variant identifiers](variants.html#catch-a-coordinate-from-the-wrong-genome-build).
